children.title: Constraint Deletion Effects
children.top_down_role: Feasibility and value consequences of removing an existing restriction.

knowledge_statements.title: Constraint Deletion Effects
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Feasible-set and optimal-value effects of deleting one affine inequality from a minimization LP.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:a_k^Tx\ge b_k,\ k=1,\ldots,m\}\), and suppose \(z^*=\min_{x\in F}c^Tx\) is finite. Deleting inequality \(a_i^Tx\ge b_i\) gives \(F_{-i}=\{x:a_k^Tx\ge b_k\text{ for }k\ne i\}\), so \(F\subseteq F_{-i}\). With \(z_{-i}=\inf_{x\in F_{-i}}c^Tx\), allowing \(z_{-i}=-\infty\), one has \(z_{-i}\le z^*\). If the deleted inequality is implied by the remaining inequalities, then \(F_{-i}=F\). When \(z_{-i}\) is finite, equality \(z_{-i}=z^*\) holds if and only if the relaxed LP has an optimizer satisfying the deleted inequality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Deleting an affine constraint enlarges the feasible set and cannot increase a minimization value. A redundant constraint has no effect, and finite value equality occurs exactly when a relaxed-model optimizer also satisfies the deleted constraint.
assumptions_latex: The LP feasible set is \(F=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:a_k^Tx\ge b_k,\ k=1,ldots,m\}\), and \(z^*=\min_{x\in F}c^Tx\) is finite.
Constraint \(a_i^Tx\ge b_i\) is deleted to form \(F_{-i}\).
The relaxed value is \(z_{-i}=\inf_{x\in F_{-i}}c^Tx\), with \(z_{-i}=-\infty\) when the relaxed LP is unbounded below.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[F\subseteq F_{-i},\qquad z_{-i}\le z^*;\qquad \bigl(a_i^Tx\ge b_i\ \forall x\in F_{-i}\bigr)\Longrightarrow F_{-i}=F\text{ and }z_{-i}=z^*.\]

notation.meaning: Original minimum and relaxed infimum under the extended-value convention.

children.title: Row Deletion Effects

knowledge_statements.title: Row Deletion Effects
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Effect of deleting one equality row from a standard-form minimization LP.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \(v=\inf\{c^{\mathsf T}x:Ax=b,\ x\ge 0\}\), and delete row \(i\). The resulting feasible set contains the original feasible set, so its value \(v_{-i}\) satisfies \(v_{-i}\le v\) whenever both values are defined. In the dual, deletion restricts the original dual feasible set \(D=\{y:A^{\mathsf T}y\le c\}\) to \(D\cap\{y:y_i=0\}\). Consequently, if an original dual optimum has \(y_i=0\), deletion leaves the optimal value unchanged; otherwise the value may decrease or become unbounded below.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Deleting an equality row enlarges the primal feasible set and forces the corresponding dual price to zero. The minimum cannot increase and is unchanged when an optimal dual price already vanishes.
assumptions_latex: \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n},\ b\in\mathbb R^m,\ c\in\mathbb R^n\).
The undeleted primal has a finite optimum and strong duality applies.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(v_{-i}\le v\), and \(y_i^*=0\) for some dual optimum \(y^*\) implies \(v_{-i}=v\).

notation.meaning: Optimal value after deleting equality row i.

knowledge_statements.title: Deletion Representation Equivalence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalent primal and dual representations of deleting a standard-form equality constraint.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Deleting row \(i\) from \(Ax=b\) is equivalent to retaining all rows and introducing a free, zero-cost variable \(s\): \[\inf\{c^{\mathsf T}x:A_{-i}x=b_{-i},\ x\ge0\}=\inf\{c^{\mathsf T}x:Ax+e_i s=b,\ x\ge0,\ s\in\mathbb R\}.\] Dualizing the free column gives the equality \(e_i^{\mathsf T}y=0\). Thus the dual representation is \[\sup\{b^{\mathsf T}y:A^{\mathsf T}y\le c,\ y_i=0\},\] which is equivalent to the dual formed directly from the row-deleted system.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Deleting row i equals adding a free zero-cost variable that absorbs its residual. In the dual, that free variable imposes the restriction that price i is zero.
assumptions_latex: \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\), and row \(i\) is an equality constraint.
Extended optimal values are used if either formulation is infeasible or unbounded.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The row-deleted, free-residual, and zero-dual-price formulations have identical feasible projections and optimal values.

knowledge_statements.title: Polyhedral RHS Value-Function Structure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extended-value structure for a standard-form minimization LP with variable right-hand side.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix \(A\) and \(c\), assume \(D=\{y:A^{\mathsf T}y\le c\}\ne\varnothing\), and define \(v(b)=\inf\{c^{\mathsf T}x:Ax=b,\ x\ge0\}\), with \(v(b)=+\infty\) when infeasible. For every feasible \(b\), strong duality gives \[v(b)=\max_{y\in D}b^{\mathsf T}y.\] Hence \(v\) is a convex polyhedral extended-real function: its epigraph is polyhedral, and on its effective domain it is piecewise linear. Its linear pieces are selected by the exposed optimal faces of the fixed dual polyhedron \(D\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With fixed technology and costs and a feasible dual, the RHS value is the support function of the dual feasible polyhedron, hence convex, polyhedral, and piecewise linear on its domain.
assumptions_latex: \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\) and \(c\in\mathbb R^n\) are fixed.
The dual feasible set \(D\) is nonempty.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(v=\sigma_D\) on the primal-feasible RHS cone, and \(v\) has polyhedral piecewise-linear structure.

knowledge_statements.title: RHS Finite-Value Domain
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Effective value domain when the fixed dual constraints are feasible.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(v(b)=\inf\{c^{\mathsf T}x:Ax=b,\ x\ge0\}\), using \(+\infty\) for infeasibility and \(-\infty\) for unboundedness. If the fixed dual set \(D=\{y:A^{\mathsf T}y\le c\}\) is nonempty, weak duality bounds every feasible primal problem below. Therefore every \(b\in\mathcal F_A=A\mathbb R_+^n\) has a finite attained value, while every \(b\notin\mathcal F_A\) has value \(+\infty\). Consequently, \[\operatorname{dom}v:=\{b:v(b)\in\mathbb R\}=\mathcal F_A.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If the fixed dual system is feasible, every feasible RHS has a finite attained optimum. Thus the finite-value domain equals the cone of feasible right-hand sides.
assumptions_latex: \(D=\{y:A^{\mathsf T}y\le c\}\ne\varnothing\).
The LP is finite-dimensional.

A feasible right-hand side \(b\in\mathcal F_A\) lies in \(\operatorname{rbd}\mathcal F_A\) exactly when there exists \(z\in\mathbb R^m\) such that \[A^{\mathsf T}z\ge0,\qquad z^{\mathsf T}b=0,\qquad z\notin L^\perp.\] For every representation \(b=Ax\) with \(x\ge0\), the equality \(0=z^{\mathsf T}b=\sum_{j=1}^n x_j z^{\mathsf T}a_j\) implies \(x_j=0\) whenever \(z^{\mathsf T}a_j>0\). knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A feasible RHS is on the relative boundary exactly when a supporting vector that is nonzero on the cone's span exposes a proper face containing it. knowledge_statements.title: RHS Linearity Regions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Normal-cone regions on which one dual optimum supplies the RHS value.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(D=\{y:A^{\mathsf T}y\le c\}\) and \(y\in D\), define its maximization normal cone by \[N_D(y):=\{b\in\mathbb R^m:b^{\mathsf T}(z-y)\le0\ \text{for every }z\in D\}.\] The RHS linearity region associated with \(y\) is \(R_y:=\operatorname{dom}v\cap N_D(y)\). These polyhedral regions cover \(\operatorname{dom}v\); overlaps correspond to right-hand sides having more than one dual optimal solution.

knowledge_statements.title: RHS Breakpoint Geometry
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Geometric description of breakpoints along an affine RHS path.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(b(t)=b_0+td\) remain in \(\operatorname{dom}v\) on an interval \(I\), and set \(g(t)=v(b(t))\). Because \(v\) is polyhedral, \(I\) admits a finite subdivision into intervals on which one exposed face of \(D\) remains optimal and \(g\) is affine. An interior parameter \(t_*\) is a breakpoint only if \(b(t_*)\) lies in the intersection of distinct RHS linearity regions. Equivalently, distinct dual optima \(y^-,y^+\) satisfy \[b(t_*)^{\mathsf T}(y^--y^+)=0,\] while their affine value functions exchange dominance at \(t_*\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Along an affine RHS path, breakpoints occur where the path crosses boundaries between dual normal-cone regions and competing dual affine valuations tie.

\(D\) is the fixed dual feasible polyhedron.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(v(b)=\max_{y\in D}b^{\mathsf T}y\) on its finite-value domain and define \(Y(b)=\operatorname*{argmax}_{y\in D}b^{\mathsf T}y\). If \(b+td\in\operatorname{dom}v\) for all sufficiently small \(t\ge0\), then the directional marginal value is \[v'(b;d)=\max_{y\in Y(b)}d^{\mathsf T}y.\] For an affine path \(b(t)=b_0+td\) that is locally contained in \(\operatorname{dom}v\), let \(g(t)=v(b(t))\). At every interior parameter \(t_*\), \[g'_-(t_*)=\min_{y\in Y(b(t_*))}d^{\mathsf T}y,\qquad g'_+(t_*)=\max_{y\in Y(b(t_*))}d^{\mathsf T}y.\] Hence a genuine marginal-value regime change occurs exactly when these extrema differ, and convexity gives \(g'_-(t_*)\le g'_+(t_*)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a feasible RHS direction, the directional marginal value is the largest directional valuation among the current dual optimizers. Along an affine RHS path, the left and right slopes are the minimum and maximum such valuations, so a genuine regime change occurs exactly when they differ.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Dual Optima as Subgradients of the LP Value Function
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterization of all optimal dual price vectors through right-hand-side sensitivity.

knowledge_statements.title: Unique Dual-Price Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Normal-cone characterization of right-hand sides having one optimal dual price vector.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D=\{y:A^{\mathsf T}y\le c\}\), and let \(y^*\) be a vertex of \(D\). The right-hand sides for which \(y^*\) is the unique dual optimal price are precisely \[U_{y^*}:=\operatorname{dom}v\cap\operatorname{ri}N_D(y^*),\] where the relative interior is taken in the linear span of the normal cone. knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A dual vertex is the unique optimal price on the relative interior of its normal cone. There the RHS value has one linear gradient, namely that price vector.

knowledge_statements.title: Multiple Dual-Price Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dual-price multiplicity for right-hand-side sensitivity in standard-form minimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider the primal-dual pair \\(v(b)=\\min\\{c^Tx:Ax=b,\\ x\\ge0\\}\\) and \\(\\max\\{b^Ty:A^Ty\\le c\\}\\), with finite attained optimum. The optimal price set is \\(Y^*(b)=\\{y:A^Ty\\le c,\\ b^Ty=v(b)\\}\\). A multiple dual-price regime occurs when \\(Y^*(b)\\) is not a singleton. It is a nonempty polyhedron, and every \\(y\\in Y^*(b)\\) supplies the global affine lower bound \\(v(b')\\ge v(b)+y^T(b'-b)\\) whenever the perturbed primal value is finite. Thus distinct optimal prices can yield distinct marginal predictions while agreeing on the current value.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Multiple optimal dual solutions agree on the present LP value but may assign different marginal values to right-hand-side perturbations.
assumptions_latex: \\(v(b)\\in\\mathbb R\\) and both primal and dual optima are attained.

knowledge_statements.title: Polyhedral Cost Value-Function Structure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Global dependence of a fixed polyhedral feasible set on its objective vector.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \\(P\\subseteq\\mathbb R^n\\) be a nonempty polytope and define \\(\\phi(c)=\\min_{x\\in P}c^Tx\\). If \\(V(P)\\) is the finite vertex set of \\(P\\), then \\[\\phi(c)=\\min_{v\\in V(P)}c^Tv.\\] Consequently, \\(\\phi\\) is finite, concave, positively homogeneous, continuous, and piecewise linear on \\(\\mathbb R^n\\). Its linearity regions are polyhedral cones of the minimization normal fan of \\(P\\), and its concave superdifferential satisfies \\(\\partial^+\\phi(c)=\\operatorname{argmin}_{x\\in P}c^Tx\\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Minimizing a varying cost over a fixed polytope gives a concave, homogeneous, piecewise-linear value function whose superdifferential is the optimal face.
assumptions_latex: \\(P\\) is a nonempty polytope in \\(\\mathbb R^n\\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \\(\\phi(c)=\\min_{v\\in V(P)}c^Tv\\) and \\(\\partial^+\\phi(c)=\\operatorname{argmin}_{x\\in P}c^Tx\\).

notation.meaning: concave superdifferential of φ at c

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Concavity and Local Linearity of the LP Cost Value Function
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Global and local behavior of the optimal value as the objective vector varies in a feasible standard-form linear program.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Consider a feasible linear program in standard form, and let $G(c)$ denote its optimal cost for objective vector $c$. Define
\[
T:=\{c\mid G(c)\text{ is finite}\}.
\]
Then $T$ is convex and $G$ is concave on $T$. Moreover, if the problem at some $\bar c$ has the unique optimal solution $x^*$, then in a neighborhood of $\bar c$,
\[
G(c)=c^{\mathsf T}x^*,
\]
and hence
\[
\nabla G(\bar c)=x^*.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a feasible standard-form linear program, the objective vectors with finite optimal cost form a convex set, and the optimal-cost function is concave on that set. If the problem has a unique optimum x* at c-bar, then nearby objective vectors have value c-transpose x*, so the gradient at c-bar is x*.
assumptions_latex: \text{The linear program in standard form is feasible.}
T=\{c\mid G(c)\text{ is finite}\}.
\text{For the local conclusion, the problem at }\bar c\text{ has the unique optimal solution }x^*.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: T\text{ is convex},\qquad G\text{ is concave on }T,\qquad G(c)=c^{\mathsf T}x^*\text{ near }\bar c\text{ under uniqueness, and }\nabla G(\bar c)=x^*.

knowledge_statements.title: Normal-Fan Cost Regions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Minimization-normal cones classify objective vectors by their optimal faces.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a nonempty polytope \\(P\\subseteq\\mathbb R^n\\) and a nonempty face \\(F\\) of \\(P\\), define its minimization normal cone by \\[N_P^-(F)=\\{c\\in\\mathbb R^n:c^T(z-x)\\ge0\\text{ for all }x\\in F,\\ z\\in P\\}.\\] Then \\(c\\in N_P^-(F)\\) exactly when every point of \\(F\\) minimizes \\(c^Tx\\) over \\(P\\), while \\(c\\in\\operatorname{ri}N_P^-(F)\\) exactly when the complete optimal set is \\(F\\). The cones \\(N_P^-(F)\\), over all nonempty faces, form a complete polyhedral fan covering \\(\\mathbb R^n\\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each normal-fan cone contains precisely the costs making a given face optimal; its relative interior selects that face as the entire optimum set.
assumptions_latex: \\(P\\) is a nonempty polytope.
\\(F\\) is a nonempty face of \\(P\\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \\(c\\in\\operatorname{ri}N_P^-(F)\\iff\\operatorname{argmin}_{x\\in P}c^Tx=F\\).

notation.meaning: minimization normal cone of face F

knowledge_statements.title: Optimal-Face Transitions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Face changes along a line through objective-coefficient space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \\(P\\) be a nonempty polytope and let \\(c(t)=c_0+td\\). The optimal-face map \\(F(t)=\\operatorname{argmin}_{x\\in P}c(t)^Tx\\) is constant on each open interval whose image lies in the relative interior of one normal-fan cone. A transition can occur only when \\(c(t)\\) meets a boundary shared by normal cones. At such a parameter, the optimal face contains the limiting optimal faces from adjacent intervals; it may therefore be higher-dimensional and represent tied vertices or faces. Only finitely many transitions occur on any bounded parameter interval unless the cost line lies in a fan boundary.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Along an affine cost path, the optimal face is piecewise constant and changes only at normal-cone boundaries, where larger tied faces may appear.
assumptions_latex: \\(P\\) is a nonempty polytope.
\\(c(t)=c_0+td\\) is an affine cost path.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \\(F(t)\\) is piecewise constant, with transitions confined to normal-fan boundaries.

knowledge_statements.title: Strictly Complementary Sensitivity Analysis
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Basis-independent local ranging through a strictly complementary primal-dual optimum.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\), \(b\in\mathbb R^m\), and \(c\in\mathbb R^n\). For \(\min\{c^Tx:Ax=b,\ x\ge0\}\), write the dual slack as \(s=c-A^Ty\ge0\). An optimal triple \((x,y,s)\) is strictly complementary when \(x_js_j=0\) and \(x_j+s_j>0\) for every \(j\). Define \(B=\{j:x_j>0\}\) and \(N=\{j:s_j>0\}\). For perturbed data \((\widetilde A,\widetilde b,\widetilde c)\) of the same dimensions, preservation of this strict partition is characterized by the existence of \(x_B,y,s_N\) satisfying \[\widetilde A_Bx_B=\widetilde b,\qquad \widetilde A_B^Ty=\widetilde c_B,\qquad \widetilde A_N^Ty+s_N=\widetilde c_N,\qquad x_B>0,\quad s_N>0,\] with \(x_N=0\) and \(s_B=0\). For each fixed parameter these are linear equations and strict sign inequalities in the primal-dual variables. If \(A\) is fixed and \(b\) and \(c\) depend affinely on the parameter, the displayed system is jointly linear in the variables and parameters.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A strictly complementary optimum defines positive primal and positive dual-slack index sets. The same partition persists exactly while the perturbed primal-dual equations admit a solution with the same strict sign pattern; joint linearity in parameters requires suitable affine data dependence.
assumptions_latex: \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\), \(b\in\mathbb R^m\), and \(c\in\mathbb R^n\).
The reference primal and dual problems have a strictly complementary optimal triple.
Perturbed problems retain the same dimensions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The strict partition \((B,N)\) is preserved exactly when the displayed perturbed primal-dual system has a solution with \(x_B>0\) and \(s_N>0\).

notation.meaning: indices positive in the strictly complementary primal solution

knowledge_statements.title: Optimal-Partition Invariancy
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Invariancy region for the maximal primal support and maximal dual-slack support.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each parameter \\(\\theta\\), consider \\(\\min\\{c(\\theta)^Tx:A(\\theta)x=b(\\theta),\\ x\\ge0\\}\\) with dual slack \\(s=c(\\theta)-A(\\theta)^Ty\\ge0\\), and assume a finite attained optimum. Define \\(B(\\theta)=\\{j:x_j>0\\text{ for some primal optimum }x\\}\\) and \\(N(\\theta)=\\{j:s_j>0\\text{ for some dual optimum }(y,s)\\}\\). By complementarity these sets are disjoint, and strict complementarity gives \\(B(\\theta)\\cup N(\\theta)=\\{1,\\ldots,n\\}\\). A set \\(R\\) is an optimal-partition invariancy region when \\((B(\\theta),N(\\theta))\\) is identical for every \\(\\theta\\in R\\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An optimal-partition invariancy region is a parameter set on which the maximal primal support and maximal positive dual-slack support remain unchanged.
assumptions_latex: For every \\(\\theta\\in R\\), primal and dual optima exist with a finite common value.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \\((B(\\theta),N(\\theta))\\) is constant on \\(R\\).

A parameter set \\(R\\) is support-set invariant for this selection when one index set \\(S\\) satisfies \\(S(\\theta)=S\\) for every \\(\\theta\\in R\\). In the selection-independent maximal-support version, define \\(S_{\\max}(\\theta)=\\{j:x_j>0\\text{ for some }x\\in X^*(\\theta)\\}\\); invariance means \\(S_{\\max}(\\theta)\\) is constant on \\(R\\). knowledge_statements.title: Classical Basis Approach
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local sensitivity ranges obtained by retaining one primal-dual optimal basis.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \\(\\min\\{c(\\theta)^Tx:A(\\theta)x=b(\\theta),\\ x\\ge0\\}\\), choose a nonsingular optimal basis \\(A_B(\\theta_0)\\). For each candidate parameter \\(\\theta\\) where \\(A_B(\\theta)\\) remains nonsingular, compute \\(x_B(\\theta)=A_B(\\theta)^{-1}b(\\theta)\\), set \\(x_N(\\theta)=0\\), compute \\(y(\\theta)=A_B(\\theta)^{-T}c_B(\\theta)\\), and form \\(r_N(\\theta)=c_N(\\theta)-A_N(\\theta)^Ty(\\theta)\\). Retain the basis while \\(x_B(\\theta)\\ge0\\) and \\(r_N(\\theta)\\ge0\\). The maximal connected parameter set containing \\(\\theta_0\\) on which these tests hold is the basis-stability range; boundary failure triggers a pivot or termination.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Fix an optimal basis, recompute its basic solution and reduced costs, and retain it exactly while primal feasibility and dual feasibility hold.
assumptions_latex: \\(A_B(\\theta_0)\\) is nonsingular and optimal at \\(\\theta_0\\).
The parameterized data permit evaluation of the displayed quantities.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The retained basis is optimal wherever \\(x_B(\\theta)\\ge0\\) and \\(r_N(\\theta)\\ge0\\).

The maximal connected parameter set containing \\(\\theta_0\\) for which this system is solvable is the strict optimal-partition invariancy region. Its boundary is reached when feasibility fails or a required positive component reaches zero.

knowledge_statements.title: Comparative Stability Coverage
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Comparison of basis-stability and optimal-partition invariancy regions under degeneracy.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix an optimal basis \\(B_0\\) at \\(\\theta_0\\), and let \\(R_{B_0}\\) be the parameters for which that basis remains primal and dual feasible. Let \\(R_{\\Pi}\\) be the parameters preserving the reference optimal partition \\(\\Pi\\). Then \\(R_{B_0}\\subseteq R_{\\Pi}\\) whenever preservation of \\(B_0\\) preserves \\(\\Pi\\). The inclusion can be strict in degenerate problems: one basis may lose feasibility while another basis represents the same optimal face and partition. If the reference optimum is a nondegenerate vertex with a locally unique optimal basis, the two approaches give the same local stability region until degeneracy, a tie, or infeasibility is encountered.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Simplex Path Algorithm for a Parametric Cost Vector
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Basis-following algorithm for a fixed-direction objective perturbation of a standard-form minimization LP.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider $\min\{(c+\lambda c')^Tx:Ax=b,\ x\ge 0\}$ for $\lambda\ge 0$, with a basis $B$ optimal at $\lambda=0$. For each current nonbasic index $j$, let $r_j(\lambda)=(z_j-c_j)+\lambda(z'_j-c'_j)$ and set $S=\{j:z'_j-c'_j>0\}$. If $S=\varnothing$, the current basic feasible solution is optimal for all larger $\lambda$. Otherwise, the next breakpoint is $\widehat\lambda=\min_{j\in S}\{- (z_j-c_j)/(z'_j-c'_j)\}$. On the interval ending at this breakpoint, the current basis is optimal and $v(\lambda)=c_B^TB^{-1}b+\lambda(c'_B)^TB^{-1}b$. At the breakpoint, a minimizing nonbasic variable enters; if a blocking basic variable exists, pivot and repeat with the updated basis. If no blocking variable exists, the LP is unbounded for every $\lambda$ strictly greater than the breakpoint.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Track the affine reduced costs as the objective vector moves along a fixed direction. The first reduced cost to reach its optimality boundary determines the next breakpoint. Pivot there and repeat. Between breakpoints the basis remains optimal and the value is affine. If no reduced cost can deteriorate, the basis stays optimal for all larger parameter values; if an entering variable has no blocking variable, the problem is unbounded beyond that breakpoint.
assumptions_latex: \lambda\ge 0.
\min\{c^Tx:Ax=b,\ x\ge 0\}\text{ has an optimal basis }B\text{ at }\lambda=0.
c\text{ is replaced by }c+\lambda c'.
r_j(\lambda)=(z_j-c_j)+\lambda(z'_j-c'_j)\text{ under the stated minimization-tableau sign convention.}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{Successive reduced-cost breakpoints and simplex pivots identify an optimal basis and affine optimal value on each parameter interval, until permanent optimality or unboundedness for all larger }\lambda\text{ is certified.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Dual-Simplex Path Algorithm for a Parametric Right-Hand Side
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Basis-following algorithm for a fixed-direction right-hand-side perturbation of a standard-form minimization LP.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider $\min\{c^Tx:Ax=b+\lambda b',\ x\ge 0\}$ for $\lambda\ge 0$, with a basis $B$ optimal at $\lambda=0$. The reduced costs are unchanged by the perturbation, while $x_B(\lambda)=B^{-1}(b+\lambda b')$ and $v(\lambda)=c_B^TB^{-1}(b+\lambda b')$. Let $\bar b=B^{-1}b$, $\bar b'=B^{-1}b'$, and $S=\{i:\bar b'_i<0\}$. If $S=\varnothing$, the current basis remains optimal for all larger $\lambda$. Otherwise, the next breakpoint is $\widehat\lambda=\min_{i\in S}\{\bar b_i/(-\bar b'_i)\}$. The current basis is optimal through this breakpoint. At the breakpoint, remove a basic variable attaining the minimum, choose an entering variable by the dual-simplex criterion, update the tableau, and repeat. The process ends when $S$ becomes empty or when the limiting row has only nonnegative coefficients; in the latter case, no feasible solution exists for any $\lambda$ strictly greater than the breakpoint.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A right-hand-side perturbation leaves reduced costs unchanged, so an optimal basis remains optimal while its parameter-dependent basic variables remain nonnegative. The first basic variable to reach zero determines a breakpoint; perform a dual-simplex pivot and repeat. If no basic variable decreases, the basis stays optimal for all larger parameters. A limiting row with no eligible entering variable certifies infeasibility beyond the breakpoint.
assumptions_latex: \lambda\ge 0.
\min\{c^Tx:Ax=b,\ x\ge 0\}\text{ has an optimal basis }B\text{ at }\lambda=0.
b\text{ is replaced by }b+\lambda b'.
c_B^TB^{-1}N-c_N^T\le 0\text{ under the stated minimization-tableau sign convention.}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{Successive primal-feasibility breakpoints and dual-simplex pivots identify the optimal basis, solution, and affine optimal value on each parameter interval, until permanent optimality or infeasibility for all larger }\lambda\text{ is certified.}

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\), \(c\in\mathbb{R}^n\), \(b\in\mathbb{R}^m\), \(E\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times k}\), and \(\theta\in\Theta\subseteq\mathbb{R}^k\). For
\[P(\theta):\quad \min\{c^{\mathsf T}x:Ax=b+E\theta,\ x\geq0\},\]
the associated parametric dual is
\[Q(\theta):\quad \max\{(b+E\theta)^{\mathsf T}y:A^{\mathsf T}y\leq c,\ y\in\mathbb{R}^m\}.\]
Thus the primal right-hand-side path becomes a dual objective path, while the dual feasible region is independent of \(\theta\). Whenever both problems are feasible, strong LP duality gives
\[v_P(\theta)=v_Q(\theta),\]
and every primal-dual optimal pair satisfies \(x_j(c_j-a_j^{\mathsf T}y)=0\) for each \(j\in\{1,\ldots,n\}\), where \(a_j\) is column \(j\) of \(A\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Dualizing a right-hand-side-parametric LP transfers the parameter into the dual objective; feasible primal-dual optima have equal values and satisfy complementary slackness.

knowledge_statements.title: Linearity Intervals
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Basis-defined interval for a scalar affine right-hand-side path with fixed matrix and objective.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Consider \(P(t)=\min\{c^{\mathsf T}x:Ax=b+td,\ x\geq0\}\), where \(A\) has full row rank. For a basis \(B\), define \(x_B(t)=A_B^{-1}(b+td)\), \(x_N(t)=0\), and \(r_N=c_N-A_N^{\mathsf T}A_B^{-\mathsf T}c_B\). A linearity interval of \(B\) is a maximal connected interval \(I_B\) on which \(x_B(t)\geq0\) and \(r_N\geq0\). On \(I_B\), this basic solution is optimal and
\[v(t)=c_B^{\mathsf T}A_B^{-1}b+t\,c_B^{\mathsf T}A_B^{-1}d,\]
so the optimal value is affine in \(t\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A linearity interval is a maximal parameter interval on which one basis remains primal and dual feasible, making the optimal value affine.
assumptions_latex: \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\) has rank \(m\).
\(A_B\) is nonsingular and \(r_N\geq0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(t\in I_B\) implies basis optimality and affine value \(v(t)=c_B^{\mathsf T}A_B^{-1}(b+td)\).

knowledge_statements.title: Optimal Sets within Linearity Intervals
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nondegenerate behavior in the interior of an RHS linearity interval.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(P(t)=\min\{c^{\mathsf T}x:Ax=b+td,\ x\geq0\}\), let basis \(B\) be valid on a linearity interval \(I_B\). If, throughout an open subinterval \(J\subseteq\operatorname{int}I_B\), one has \(A_B^{-1}(b+td)>0\) and \(r_N>0\), then the primal optimum is unique and equals
\[x_B^*(t)=A_B^{-1}(b+td),\qquad x_N^*(t)=0.\]
The dual optimum is unique and constant on \(J\), namely \(y^*=A_B^{-\mathsf T}c_B\). Hence the primal optimal solution varies affinely, the dual optimal solution remains fixed, and neither optimal set changes dimension inside \(J\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under strict basic positivity and strict reduced costs, an interval has unique optima: the primal solution varies affinely and the dual solution stays constant.

\(A_B^{-1}(b+td)>0\) and \(r_N>0\) for every \(t\in J\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(X^*(t)=\{x^*(t)\}\) and \(Y^*(t)=\{A_B^{-\mathsf T}c_B\}\) for all \(t\in J\).

Let \(P(t)\) be an LP whose data depend continuously on scalar \(t\), and let \(t_*\) separate two linearity intervals. Suppose optimal solutions \(x^-(t)\) and \(x^+(t)\) on the respective sides have finite limits \(\bar x^-\) and \(\bar x^+\), and the optimal value is finite and continuous at \(t_*\). Then both limits are feasible and optimal for \(P(t_*)\). Consequently,
\[\operatorname{conv}\{\bar x^-,\bar x^+\}\subseteq X^*(t_*).\]
The analogous inclusion holds for finite one-sided limits of dual optima. Thus a breakpoint optimal set can strictly contain the optimal sets occurring immediately on either side.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Finite one-sided limits of adjacent optimal solutions are optimal at the breakpoint, and their convex hull lies in the breakpoint optimal set.
assumptions_latex: The LP data and finite optimal value are continuous at \(t_*\).
The stated one-sided optimal-solution limits exist and are finite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{conv}\{\bar x^-,\bar x^+\}\subseteq X^*(t_*)\), with the corresponding dual inclusion.

knowledge_statements.title: Linearity-Interval Endpoints
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Ratio representation of the maximal feasibility interval for a fixed basis.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For an RHS path and fixed dual-feasible basis \(B\), write
\[x_B(t)=A_B^{-1}(b+td)=\alpha+t\beta.\]
The basis-validity interval is \(I_B=[t_-,t_+]\), where
\[t_- =\max_{i:\beta_i>0}\left(-\frac{\alpha_i}{\beta_i}\right),\qquad t_+=\min_{i:\beta_i<0}\left(-\frac{\alpha_i}{\beta_i}\right).\]
The maximum over an empty set is \(-\infty\), and the minimum over an empty set is \(+\infty\). The basis is primal feasible exactly when \(t\in I_B\). Every finite endpoint is attained by at least one index \(i\) satisfying \(\alpha_i+t\beta_i=0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A basis interval’s endpoints are the tightest componentwise ratio bounds obtained from nonnegativity of its affine basic solution.
assumptions_latex: \(A_B\) is nonsingular.
The fixed basis is dual feasible.
\(I_B\neq\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(I_B=\{t:\alpha+t\beta\geq0\}=[t_-,t_+]\) with the displayed ratio endpoints.

children.title: Primal-Feasibility Breakpoints
children.top_down_role: Transitions associated with loss of current primal feasibility.

knowledge_statements.title: Primal-Feasibility Breakpoints
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Endpoint condition caused by loss of nonnegativity of the current basic solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For an RHS path, let the current dual-feasible basis satisfy \(x_B(t)=\alpha+t\beta\geq0\) on an interval ending at finite \(t_*\). The endpoint \(t_*\) is a primal-feasibility breakpoint in direction \(\sigma\in\{-1,1\}\) if
\[\min_i(\alpha_i+t_*\beta_i)=0\]
and there exists an active index \(i\) with \(\alpha_i+t_*\beta_i=0\) and \(\sigma\beta_i<0\). Then for every sufficiently small \(\varepsilon>0\), the current basic solution at \(t_*+\sigma\varepsilon\) has a negative component and the basis is no longer primal feasible.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A primal-feasibility breakpoint occurs when a basic variable reaches zero and would become negative if the parameter continued in the chosen direction.
assumptions_latex: \(x_B(t)=\alpha+t\beta\) is feasible up to \(t_*\).
The basis remains dual feasible at \(t_*\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x_B(t_*+\sigma\varepsilon)\not\geq0\) for all sufficiently small \(\varepsilon>0\).

children.title: Dual-Optimality Breakpoints
children.top_down_role: Transitions associated with loss of current dual optimality.

knowledge_statements.title: Dual-Optimality Breakpoints
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Endpoint condition caused by loss of nonnegativity of a current reduced cost.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Consider the objective path \(P(t)=\min\{(c+tq)^{\mathsf T}x:Ax=b,\ x\geq0\}\) and a primal-feasible basis \(B\). Define
\[y(t)=A_B^{-\mathsf T}(c_B+tq_B),\qquad r_N(t)=c_N+tq_N-A_N^{\mathsf T}y(t)=\rho+t\eta.\]
A finite endpoint \(t_*\) is a dual-optimality breakpoint in direction \(\sigma\in\{-1,1\}\) if \(r_N(t_*)\geq0\) and some \(j\in N\) satisfies \(r_j(t_*)=0\) and \(\sigma\eta_j<0\). Then \(r_j(t_*+\sigma\varepsilon)<0\) for every sufficiently small \(\varepsilon>0\), so the current basis ceases to be dual feasible and hence ceases to certify optimality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A dual-optimality breakpoint occurs when a reduced cost reaches zero and would turn negative as the objective parameter continues.
assumptions_latex: \(A_B\) is nonsingular and the basis is primal feasible.
\(r_N(t)\geq0\) up to \(t_*\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(r_N(t_*+\sigma\varepsilon)\not\geq0\) for all sufficiently small \(\varepsilon>0\).

knowledge_statements.title: Simultaneous Breakpoint Events
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Multiple primal or dual boundary inequalities become active at the same parameter value.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a basis along a scalar affine parameter path, collect its primal and dual validity slacks into \(s(t)\), with basis optimality equivalent to \(s(t)\geq0\). A breakpoint \(t_*\) is simultaneous when
\[\left|\{i:s_i(t_*)=0\ \text{and}\ \sigma s_i'(t_*)<0\}\right|\geq2\]
for the continuation direction \(\sigma\in\{-1,1\}\). The active indices may comprise several basic variables, several reduced costs, or both types. Consequently, more than one feasibility or optimality boundary blocks continuation of the current basis at exactly the same parameter value.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A simultaneous breakpoint occurs when at least two basic-variable or reduced-cost boundaries obstruct the current basis at the same parameter value.
assumptions_latex: Each validity slack is affine in scalar \(t\).
The current basis is optimal on the approaching side of \(t_*\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: At least two components of \(s(t)\) become directionally violating at the common breakpoint \(t_*\).

children.title: Degenerate Breakpoint Events
children.top_down_role: Breakpoint regimes shaped by degenerate basis or solution structure.

knowledge_statements.title: Degenerate Breakpoint Events
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Breakpoint event involving a zero basic variable or a zero-length pivot step.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
At a breakpoint \(t_*\), an optimal basis \(B\) is primal degenerate when
\[x_B(t_*)\geq0,\qquad \left|\{i\in B:x_i(t_*)=0\}\right|\geq1.\]
A breakpoint pivot is degenerate when its admissible primal step length is zero; equivalently, the leaving basic variable is already zero before the pivot displacement. Such a pivot can replace the basis without changing the represented primal point or the optimal value at \(t_*\). Therefore a basis change at a degenerate breakpoint need not identify a new optimal solution, a new value-function slope, or a distinct linearity regime.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At a degenerate breakpoint, a zero basic variable permits a zero-step pivot, so the basis may change without changing the solution or value.
assumptions_latex: \(B\) is an optimal basis at \(t_*\).
A valid simplex pivot is available at the active boundary.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A zero-step pivot may change \(B\) while leaving \(x^*(t_*)\) and \(v(t_*)\) unchanged.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nonuniqueness of the adjacent continuation basis when multiple pivot resolutions remain valid on the continuation side of a breakpoint.

source_refs.locator: 3. The Parametric Self-Dual Simplex Method p. 116

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(t_*\) be a simultaneous or degenerate breakpoint for an optimal basis \(B\), and fix a continuation direction \(\sigma\in\{-1,1\}\). Suppose the breakpoint ratio test admits two distinct valid pivot resolutions producing bases \(B_1\neq B_2\), and that both bases are primal and dual feasible for every \(t=t_*+\sigma\varepsilon\) with all sufficiently small \(\varepsilon>0\). Then the active equalities
\[\{i:x_i(t_*)=0\},\qquad \{j:r_j(t_*)=0\}\]
do not determine a unique leaving variable, entering variable, or adjacent optimal basis. A tie-breaking rule or perturbation convention is required to select a single basis path, although the LP optimal set and optimal value at each parameter remain well defined.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When distinct pivots produce bases that both remain optimal immediately beyond a degenerate or simultaneous breakpoint, the active constraints alone cannot determine a unique adjacent basis.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Finite Correctness of Objective-Parametric Breakpoint Tracing
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite termination and output characterization for the preceding scalar objective-parametric path algorithm.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $g(\gamma)=\min\{(c+\gamma\Delta c)^Tx:Ax=b,\ x\geq0\}$ for $\gamma\geq0$, and let $(\gamma_k,x^k,y^k,s^k)$ be generated by the preceding breakpoint-tracing algorithm. The algorithm terminates after finitely many iterations. If $K$ is its number of iterations, then $\gamma_1,\ldots,\gamma_K$ are the successive breakpoints of $g$ on the nonnegative real line, $g(\gamma_k)=b^Ty^k$ for $1\leq k\leq K$, and the slope of $g$ on $(\gamma_k,\gamma_{k+1})$ is $\Delta c^Tx^k$ for $1\leq k<K$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The objective-parametric path algorithm terminates finitely. Its generated parameters are the successive nonnegative breakpoints; the dual objective gives the value at each breakpoint, and the directional primal objective gives the slope between consecutive breakpoints.

children.title: Primal Parametric Simplex Methods
children.top_down_role: Path methods organized around primal-feasible basis transitions.

knowledge_statements.title: Primal Parametric Simplex Methods
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scalar parametric simplex continuation through primal-feasible optimal bases.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider the minimization LP \(\min\{c(\theta)^T x:Ax=b,\ x\geq0\}\), where \(c(\theta)=c^0+\theta d\). Start at an optimal primal-feasible basis \(B\) for \(\theta_0\). While \(x_B=A_B^{-1}b\geq0\), compute \(y(\theta)=A_B^{-T}c_B(\theta)\) and \(r_N(\theta)=c_N(\theta)-A_N^Ty(\theta)\). Advance \(\theta\) to the smallest larger value at which some component of \(r_N(\theta)\) becomes zero. Perform a primal-simplex pivot with an entering index attaining zero reduced cost and a ratio-test leaving index, retaining primal feasibility. Stop at the parameter endpoint or when no admissible pivot exists; output the visited optimality intervals and bases.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Maintain primal feasibility, advance until a reduced cost vanishes, pivot by the primal simplex rule, and record successive optimal-basis intervals.
assumptions_latex: \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\) has full row rank.
An optimal primal-feasible basis is known at \(\theta_0\).
A consistent anti-cycling rule resolves degeneracy.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: On every traversed interval, the current basis is primal feasible and dual feasible, hence optimal.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm kind and primal-feasible path-method placement are correct, but no inspectable source is supplied. An authoritative reference must also confirm the directional entering-variable rule at a reduced-cost breakpoint, since choosing an arbitrary index whose reduced cost is zero need not produce a basis valid immediately to the right.

knowledge_statements.title: Dual Parametric Simplex Methods
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scalar parametric continuation through dual-feasible optimal bases.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \(\min\{c^Tx:Ax=b(\theta),\ x\geq0\}\), where \(b(\theta)=b^0+\theta h\). Start at an optimal basis \(B\) for \(\theta_0\). Its reduced costs \(r_N=c_N-A_N^TA_B^{-T}c_B\) are independent of \(\theta\) and remain nonnegative. Advance \(\theta\) until the first component of \(x_B(\theta)=A_B^{-1}b(\theta)\) reaches zero. If continuation makes that component negative, apply a dual-simplex pivot: choose the leaving row from the violated basic variables and an entering column by the dual ratio test so that the new reduced costs remain nonnegative. Stop at the endpoint or when no entering column exists; output the traversed intervals and bases.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Preserve dual feasibility, advance until a basic variable reaches zero, then use a dual-simplex pivot to restore primal feasibility.
assumptions_latex: \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\) has full row rank.
An optimal basis is known at \(\theta_0\).
A consistent anti-cycling rule resolves degeneracy.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Each accepted basis is optimal throughout the interval where \(A_B^{-1}b(\theta)\geq0\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm kind and dual-feasible path-method placement are appropriate. No source supports the precise breakpoint and dual-ratio-test formulation, including how the continuation direction determines the leaving row and how degeneracy is handled.

children.title: Parametric Self-Dual Simplex Methods
children.top_down_role: Joint primal-dual parameter continuation and initialization.

knowledge_statements.title: Parametric Self-Dual Simplex Methods
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Joint primal-dual homotopy initialized without a feasible basis.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Embed a primal-dual LP pair in an affine family indexed by \(\lambda\geq0\), choosing perturbations so that a prescribed complementary basis is primal and dual feasible at an initial \(\lambda_0\). Decrease \(\lambda\) while solving the basis equations for primal variables, dual variables, and reduced costs. At the first value where a basic primal variable or nonbasic reduced cost reaches zero, pivot between complementary indices and continue with a basis feasible on both sides of the primal-dual system. Terminate when \(\lambda=0\), returning an optimal solution of the original pair, or return the infeasibility or unboundedness status exposed by the terminal tableau.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Follow an artificial primal-dual parameter from an easily initialized complementary basis to the original LP, pivoting at feasibility breakpoints.
assumptions_latex: The embedding depends affinely on \(\lambda\).
The initial perturbation produces a complementary primal-dual feasible basis.
Degenerate pivots use a finite anti-cycling rule.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Reaching \(\lambda=0\) with primal and dual feasibility yields an optimal primal-dual pair for the original LP.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Parametric self-dual simplex pivot algorithm
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Basis-pivot procedure for joint primal-dual parameter continuation in linear programming. The extract specifies a loop condition but does not establish finite termination or state tie and exceptional-ratio conventions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For the current basis and affine primal-dual coefficients, compute
\[
\mu^*=\max\left\{\max_{\substack{j\in\mathcal N\\ \bar z_j>0}}-\frac{z_j^*}{\bar z_j},\;\max_{\substack{i\in\mathcal B\\ \bar x_i>0}}-\frac{x_i^*}{\bar x_i}\right\}.
\]
While \(\mu^*>0\), select an index attaining this maximum. If it is \(j\in\mathcal N\), compute \(\Delta x_{\mathcal B}=B^{-1}Ne_j\), select
\[
i\in\operatorname*{argmax}_{i\in\mathcal B}\frac{\Delta x_i}{x_i^*+\mu^*\bar x_i},
\]
and compute \(\Delta z_{\mathcal N}=-(B^{-1}N)^Te_i\). If the attaining index is \(i\in\mathcal B\), compute \(\Delta z_{\mathcal N}=-(B^{-1}N)^Te_i\), select
\[
j\in\operatorname*{argmax}_{j\in\mathcal N}\frac{\Delta z_j}{z_j^*+\mu^*\bar z_j},
\]
and compute \(\Delta x_{\mathcal B}=B^{-1}Ne_j\). Set
\[
t=\frac{x_i^*}{\Delta x_i},\quad \bar t=\frac{\bar x_i}{\Delta x_i},\quad s=\frac{z_j^*}{\Delta z_j},\quad \bar s=\frac{\bar z_j}{\Delta z_j},
\]
then update
\[
x_j^*\leftarrow t,\quad \bar x_j\leftarrow\bar t,\quad z_i^*\leftarrow s,\quad \bar z_i\leftarrow\bar s,
\]
\[
x_{\mathcal B}^*\leftarrow x_{\mathcal B}^*-t\Delta x_{\mathcal B},\quad \bar x_{\mathcal B}\leftarrow\bar x_{\mathcal B}-\bar t\Delta x_{\mathcal B},
\]
\[
z_{\mathcal N}^*\leftarrow z_{\mathcal N}^*-s\Delta z_{\mathcal N},\quad \bar z_{\mathcal N}\leftarrow\bar z_{\mathcal N}-\bar s\Delta z_{\mathcal N}.
\]
Replace \(\mathcal B\) by \((\mathcal B\setminus\{i\})\cup\{j\}\), recompute \(\mu^*\), and continue while \(\mu^*>0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Compute the largest parameter obstruction among the affine primal basic and dual nonbasic variables. While it is positive, use an attaining index to form one pivot direction, select the complementary pivot index by the displayed maximum-ratio rule, form the other direction, update the constant and parameter coefficients, exchange the basis indices, and recompute the obstruction. The extract gives no finite-termination guarantee.
assumptions_latex: B\text{ is nonsingular, with basic and nonbasic index sets }\mathcal B\text{ and }\mathcal N.
(x^*,\bar x,z^*,\bar z)\text{ are the current affine primal-dual coefficients.}
\text{Each maximum, ratio selection, and pivot quotient used by the displayed procedure is well-defined.}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{The procedure continues exactly while }\mu^*>0\text{; if the loop exits, then }\mu^*\le 0.

children.title: Homotopy Path Frameworks
children.top_down_role: Parameterized deformation frameworks connecting LP instances.

knowledge_statements.title: Homotopy Path Frameworks
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Affine homotopy representation of a parametric LP path.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P_0\) be an LP with known solution structure and \(P_1\) the target LP. An affine LP homotopy is the family \(P(t)\), \(t\in[0,1]\), whose data satisfy \((A(t),b(t),c(t))=(1-t)(A_0,b_0,c_0)+t(A_1,b_1,c_1)\). For every interval on which one basis \(B\) remains nonsingular, primal and dual basic quantities are obtained from \(A_B(t)x_B(t)=b(t)\) and \(A_B(t)^Ty(t)=c_B(t)\). The valid segment consists of parameters satisfying \(x_B(t)\geq0\) and \(c_N(t)-A_N(t)^Ty(t)\geq0\); its boundary determines the next basis event.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Interpolate from a solved LP to a target LP and follow each basis while its primal and dual optimality inequalities remain valid.
assumptions_latex: The LP data vary affinely with \(t\in[0,1]\).
The active basis matrix is nonsingular on the segment considered.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The optimal path is assembled from basis-valid segments separated by feasibility, optimality, or singularity events.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Representation is a suitable kind for this homotopy framework, and the fixed-basis equations are coherent even when the basis matrix varies with the parameter. A source is required for the claimed general framework and for assembling the optimal path when feasibility, optimality, or basis singularity events occur.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Homotopy Method
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conceptual definition in an LP context; the efficiency remark is qualitative and does not assert universal effectiveness, convergence, or a complexity bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A homotopy method constructs a continuous deformation \(\{P(t):t\in[0,1]\}\) between a problem \(P(0)\) having a known trivial solution and the difficult target problem \(P(1)\), and attempts to solve the target by proceeding through the intervening problems from \(t=0\) to \(t=1\). The continuum of intermediate problems means that the technique need not be effective in every setting, although it can yield efficient algorithms for linear programming and other suitable problem domains.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A homotopy method continuously deforms a trivially solved problem into a difficult target problem and attempts to reach the target by solving or tracking the intervening problems. Because there is a continuum of intermediate problems, the technique is not effective in every setting, although it can yield efficient algorithms for linear programming and other suitable domains.
assumptions_latex: \{P(t):t\in[0,1]\}\text{ is a continuous deformation of related problem instances}
P(0)\text{ has a known trivial solution and }P(1)\text{ is the difficult target problem}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{The method attempts to solve }P(1)\text{ by continuation from }P(0)\text{, without a universal effectiveness guarantee.}

children.title: Continuation Path Frameworks
children.top_down_role: Path-following frameworks starting from a known LP instance.

knowledge_statements.title: Continuation Path Frameworks
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Event-driven local continuation of an optimal LP solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given an optimal primal-dual solution and basis at parameter \(\theta_k\), solve the differentiated basis equations to obtain the local variation of basic variables, multipliers, and reduced costs. Determine the largest step \(\Delta_k>0\) for which primal feasibility, dual feasibility, and basis nonsingularity hold on \([\theta_k,\theta_k+\Delta_k]\). Set \(\theta_{k+1}=\theta_k+\Delta_k\). If an inequality becomes tight, update the active basis by an admissible pivot; if the basis becomes singular or no admissible update exists, report a path failure. Repeat until the requested endpoint is reached, and output the ordered path segments and event parameters.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Predict the local solution path, step to its first validity event, correct the basis, and repeat until the endpoint or failure.
assumptions_latex: The LP data are continuously differentiable in the scalar parameter.
A primal-dual optimal basis is available at the initial parameter.
Local event times can be computed exactly or conservatively.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every accepted segment satisfies the primal-dual optimality conditions throughout its reported parameter interval.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Algorithm is the correct container role, but the formulation is not reliable without a source. For merely continuously differentiable LP data, solving differentiated basis equations at one parameter gives local derivatives but does not by itself determine the largest interval on which feasibility and nonsingularity hold.

children.title: Path Failure Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Structural regimes where path tracking becomes ambiguous or incomplete.

knowledge_statements.title: Path Failure Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Loss of a continuous single-valued optimizer at degeneracy.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the parametric LP \(\min\{\theta x:0\leq x\leq1\}\), the unique optimizer is \(x^*(\theta)=1\) when \(\theta<0\) and \(x^*(\theta)=0\) when \(\theta>0\), while every \(x\in[0,1]\) is optimal at \(\theta=0\). Consequently, no continuous single-valued optimizer selection can agree with the unique optimizers on both punctured sides of zero. Thus a continuation framework requiring a unique continuous primal path reaches a failure boundary at \(\theta=0\), although the optimal value and the set-valued solution map remain well defined.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A degenerate parameter can destroy every continuous single-valued optimizer path even though optimal solutions and the value remain well defined.
assumptions_latex: The continuation rule must select one optimizer and must agree with unique optimizers away from the breakpoint.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: At \(\theta=0\), uniqueness and continuous single-valued continuation fail.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The counterexample is mathematically coherent and failure_boundary is exactly the appropriate content kind: the forced one-sided selections have incompatible limits at zero. The record nevertheless supplies neither a citation nor an explicit standard-field rationale, so its evidentiary requirement is unmet.

children.title: Complete Breakpoint Traversal
children.top_down_role: Enumeration of successive intervals and breakpoints along a scalar path.

knowledge_statements.title: Complete Breakpoint Traversal
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exhaustive scalar traversal of maximal optimal-basis intervals.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a scalar interval \([\underline\theta,\overline\theta]\) and an optimal basis at \(\underline\theta\), compute the maximal parameter interval on which its basic variables and reduced costs satisfy primal-dual feasibility. Record that interval and every finite endpoint. At a right endpoint, enumerate all admissible pivots associated with newly tight basic variables or reduced costs, use a deterministic anti-cycling rule to select a basis valid immediately to the right, and continue. Terminate upon reaching \(\overline\theta\), detecting infeasibility or unboundedness, or exhausting admissible successor bases. The output is the ordered list of maximal intervals, breakpoints, and associated optimal bases.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Repeatedly extend each optimal basis to its maximal interval, pivot at the endpoint, and enumerate all breakpoints up to the requested parameter bound.
assumptions_latex: The LP data depend affinely on one scalar parameter.
Only finitely many bases exist.
Exact comparisons and a finite anti-cycling rule are used.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If every finite breakpoint has an admissible successor, the output covers \([\underline\theta,\overline\theta]\) without missing an optimality interval.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Algorithm is appropriate for complete breakpoint traversal, but no source establishes the completeness conclusion. At a degenerate breakpoint, several zero-length pivots or alternative optimal bases may be needed before obtaining a basis valid immediately to the right; finiteness of the basis set and an anti-cycling rule alone do not justify the stated coverage guarantee.

children.title: Multiparametric LP Geometry
children.top_down_role: Polyhedral subdivision of vector-parameter spaces by invariant optimal structure.

top_down_textbook_witnesses.locator: Parametric LP survey

children.title: Critical Regions
children.top_down_role: Parameter regions sharing a common optimal structure.

knowledge_statements.title: Critical Regions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Basis-defined optimality regions for an affine multiparametric LP.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(\min\{(c+F\theta)^Tx:Ax=b+E\theta,\ x\geq0\}\) with \(\theta\in\Theta\subseteq\mathbb{R}^p\), let \(B\) be a nonsingular basis and \(N\) its complement. The critical region associated with \(B\) is \[\mathcal C_B=\{\theta\in\Theta:A_B^{-1}(b+E\theta)\geq0,\ c_N+F_N\theta-A_N^TA_B^{-T}(c_B+F_B\theta)\geq0\}.\] Thus \(\mathcal C_B\) is the set of parameters for which the basic solution \(x_B(\theta)=A_B^{-1}(b+E\theta)\), \(x_N(\theta)=0\), and its induced dual solution satisfy primal and dual feasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A critical region contains exactly the parameters for which one fixed basis supplies a primal-dual optimal solution.
assumptions_latex: \(A_B\) is nonsingular.
The parameter domain \(\Theta\) is polyhedral.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The set \(\mathcal C_B\) is polyhedral and basis \(B\) is optimal for every \(\theta\in\mathcal C_B\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Definition is the correct kind and the displayed primal and reduced-cost inequalities correctly define the basis-optimality region for the stated standard-form multiparametric LP. A specific multiparametric-LP source is still required because the record contains no citation or explicit standard-field rationale.

children.title: Critical-Region Adjacency Geometry
children.top_down_role: Boundary and neighbor relations among parameter regions.

children.title: Critical-Region Facets
children.top_down_role: Boundary faces of critical regions in parameter space.

knowledge_statements.title: Critical-Region Facets
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Codimension-one boundary faces of full-dimensional critical regions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^p\) be a full-dimensional critical region represented irredundantly as \(\mathcal C=\{\theta:H\theta\leq h\}\). For row \(i\), the associated face is \(F_i=\{\theta\in\mathcal C:H_i\theta=h_i\}\). It is a critical-region facet when it is nonempty and \(\dim(F_i)=p-1\). In a basis representation of a multiparametric LP, such a facet is commonly generated by one primal-feasibility or reduced-cost inequality becoming tight, although several inequalities may define the same facet under degeneracy or redundancy.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A critical-region facet is a nonempty codimension-one face obtained by making an irredundant regional inequality tight.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal C\) is a full-dimensional polyhedron in \(\mathbb{R}^p\).
The inequality representation is irredundant.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Each facet is a maximal proper face of dimension \(p-1\).

notation.meaning: row i of the regional inequality matrix

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Definition is the correct role for this leaf, and the codimension-one face characterization is internally consistent under the full-dimensional and irredundant-representation assumptions. No inspectable source is supplied for its use as critical-region terminology.

children.title: Critical-Region Adjacency
children.top_down_role: Neighbor relations among critical regions.

knowledge_statements.title: Critical-Region Adjacency
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Facet adjacency within a full-dimensional critical-region complex.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal C_1,\mathcal C_2\subseteq\mathbb{R}^p\) be distinct full-dimensional critical regions. They are facet-adjacent when \(F=\mathcal C_1\cap\mathcal C_2\) is nonempty, \(\dim(F)=p-1\), and \(F\) is a facet of both regions. The critical-region adjacency graph has one vertex for each full-dimensional region and an undirected edge between every facet-adjacent pair. Intersections of dimension at most \(p-2\) do not establish facet adjacency, even if the closures of the two regions meet.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two full-dimensional critical regions are adjacent when their intersection is a common codimension-one facet, not merely a lower-dimensional contact.
assumptions_latex: The critical regions are full-dimensional polyhedra in a common parameter space \(\mathbb{R}^p\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Facet adjacency defines the edges of the critical-region adjacency graph.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Definition is appropriate and correctly distinguishes common-facet adjacency from lower-dimensional contact. The claim lacks a cited source or explicit standard-field rationale.

children.title: Facet-Induced Neighbor Relations
children.top_down_role: Adjacency structure arising from shared critical-region facets.

knowledge_statements.title: Facet-Induced Neighbor Relations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Neighboring bases across a nondegenerate critical-region facet.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let two full-dimensional critical regions \(\mathcal C_B\) and \(\mathcal C_{B'}\) of a nondegenerate multiparametric LP share the relative interior of a facet \(F\). Suppose exactly one basis-optimality inequality becomes tight on \(F\), and no other primal variable or reduced cost vanishes there. Then crossing \(F\) changes the optimal basis by one admissible simplex pivot: \(B'=(B\setminus\{i\})\cup\{j\}\) for one leaving index \(i\) and one entering index \(j\). Hence the shared facet induces a neighbor relation between the two basis-labeled critical regions. Under degeneracy, several bases or regions may meet the same facet, so this one-pivot correspondence need not be unique.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Across a nondegenerate facet with one tight event, neighboring critical regions have bases differing by one simplex pivot; degeneracy can destroy uniqueness.
assumptions_latex: The adjacent regions are full-dimensional.
Exactly one independent optimality inequality becomes tight on the shared facet.
The LP is primal and dual nondegenerate near the facet interior.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The two regional bases differ by a single entering-leaving exchange.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Property is the appropriate content kind, but the one-pivot neighbor conclusion is theorem-like and requires a source stating sufficient regularity and nondegeneracy assumptions. The current phrase that one basis-optimality inequality becomes tight does not independently establish the claimed correspondence without that result.

children.title: Piecewise-Affine Solution Maps
children.top_down_role: Regional organization of selected primal and dual solutions.

knowledge_statements.title: Piecewise-Affine Solution Maps
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Regional affine formulas for selected primal and dual optimizers.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(\min\{(c+F\theta)^Tx:Ax=b+E\theta,\ x\geq0\}\), fix a critical region \(\mathcal C_B\) with nonsingular basis \(B\). On that region, the basis-selected primal and dual solutions satisfy \[x_B(	heta)=A_B^{-1}(b+E	heta),\qquad x_N(	heta)=0,\qquad y_B(	heta)=A_B^{-T}(c_B+F_B	heta).\] Therefore each selected solution is affine in \(\theta\) on \(\mathcal C_B\). Since an LP has finitely many bases, any consistent basis selection over the feasible parameter domain is piecewise affine on a finite family of critical regions; degeneracy may make the optimizer set-valued and the regional representation nonunique.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A fixed optimal basis gives affine primal and dual solutions; finitely many basis regions therefore produce a piecewise-affine selected solution map.
assumptions_latex: The LP data depend affinely on \(\theta\).
Every selected regional basis matrix is nonsingular.
A consistent optimal-basis selection is specified at overlaps.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The selected primal and dual solution maps are affine on each critical region and piecewise affine over their finite union.

notation.meaning: critical region associated with basis B

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Property is appropriate, and the fixed-basis primal and dual formulas are affine. However, the dual vector should ordinarily be denoted y(theta), not y_B(theta), because its components are indexed by constraint rows rather than the basic columns. Moreover, an arbitrary 'consistent basis selection' on degenerate overlaps does not automatically yield a conventionally piecewise-affine map without a finite regional selection rule. A source is needed before choosing the precise corrected formulation.

children.title: Noncanonical Critical-Region Family
children.top_down_role: Regional descriptions complicated by nonunique bases or optimal sets.

children.title: Degenerate Critical Regions
children.top_down_role: Critical regions affected by nonunique basis or optimal structure.

knowledge_statements.title: Degenerate Critical Regions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Primal or dual basis degeneracy in a standard-form multiparametric LP.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P(\theta)=\min\{c(\theta)^\top x:Ax=b(\theta),\ x\geq0\}\) for \(\theta\in\Theta\), where \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\) has rank \(m\), \(b:\Theta\to\mathbb R^m\) and \(c:\Theta\to\mathbb R^n\) are affine, and \(\Theta\) is polyhedral. For a basis \(B\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}\) with \(|B|=m\) and nonsingular \(A_B\), let \(N=\{1,\ldots,n\}\setminus B\), \(x_B(\theta)=A_B^{-1}b(\theta)\), \(r_N(\theta)=c_N(\theta)-A_N^\top A_B^{-\top}c_B(\theta)\), and \(\mathcal R_B=\{\theta\in\Theta:x_B(\theta)\geq0,\ r_N(\theta)\geq0\}\). The basis is primal-degenerate at \(\theta\in\mathcal R_B\) if \(x_{B,i}(\theta)=0\) for some \(i\in B\), and dual-degenerate there if \(r_j(\theta)=0\) for some \(j\in N\). The basis-induced critical region is called degenerate when one of these conditions holds at some \(\theta\in\operatorname{ri}(\mathcal R_B)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A basis-induced critical region is degenerate when, at a relative-interior parameter, one of its basic variables or nonbasic reduced costs is zero.
assumptions_latex: \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\) has rank \(m\).
\(b:\Theta\to\mathbb R^m\) and \(c:\Theta\to\mathbb R^n\) are affine on a polyhedral set \(\Theta\).
\(B\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}\), \(|B|=m\), and \(A_B\) is nonsingular.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{ri}(\mathcal R_B)\cap\left(\bigcup_{i\in B}\{\theta:x_{B,i}(\theta)=0\}\cup\bigcup_{j\in N}\{\theta:r_j(\theta)=0\}\right)\neq\varnothing\).

notation.meaning: critical region induced by basis B

children.title: Overlapping Critical Regions
children.top_down_role: Regional descriptions with intersecting parameter-space coverage.

knowledge_statements.title: Overlapping Critical Regions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Overlap of basis-induced regions in degenerate multiparametric LPs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P(\theta)=\min\{c(\theta)^\top x:Ax=b(\theta),\ x\geq0\}\) for \(\theta\in\Theta\). For every nonsingular basis \(B\), let \(x^B(\theta)\) be its associated basic solution and let \(\mathcal R_B\subseteq\Theta\) be the set on which that solution is primal feasible and the corresponding reduced costs are dual feasible. Distinct bases \(B_1\neq B_2\) may satisfy \(\mathcal R_{B_1}\cap\mathcal R_{B_2}\neq\varnothing\). For every \(\theta\) in this intersection, both basic solutions are optimal for \(P(\theta)\) and have the same objective value. If the intersection has nonempty relative interior, the basis-indexed family is not a disjoint polyhedral subdivision.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Distinct optimal bases can be valid on the same parameters. Their basic solutions are optimal with equal objective values, and a relative-interior overlap makes the basis-indexed family nondisjoint.
assumptions_latex: \(P(\theta)=\min\{c(\theta)^\top x:Ax=b(\theta),\ x\geq0\}\) is the same finite-dimensional standard-form LP for all compared bases.
\(B_1\) and \(B_2\) are nonsingular bases.
\(\mathcal R_B\) is defined by primal and dual feasibility of basis \(B\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\theta\in\mathcal R_{B_1}\cap\mathcal R_{B_2}\Rightarrow x^{B_1}(\theta),x^{B_2}(\theta)\in\operatorname*{argmin}P(\theta)\) and \(c(\theta)^\top x^{B_1}(\theta)=c(\theta)^\top x^{B_2}(\theta)\).

notation.meaning: parameter region on which basis B is primal-dual feasible

source_refs.locator: Chapter 7. Sensitivity and Parametric Analyses p. 109

source_witnesses.locator: Chapter 7. Sensitivity and Parametric Analyses p. 109

children.title: Nonminimal Critical Regions
children.top_down_role: Regional descriptions containing redundant subdivisions or inequalities.

knowledge_statements.title: Nonminimal Critical Regions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Minimality relative to a family representing the same optimal-solution graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\{(\mathcal R_k,S_k)\}_{k\in K}\) represent an optimal-solution mapping by \(S(\theta)=\bigcup_{k:\theta\in\mathcal R_k}S_k(\theta)\). A member \((\mathcal R_k,S_k)\) is nonminimal if deleting it leaves this represented mapping unchanged on the parameter domain. Equivalently, for every \(\theta\in\mathcal R_k\), all solutions contributed by \(S_k(\theta)\) are already contributed by other members whose regions contain \(\theta\). Nonminimality concerns the regional family, not merely redundant inequalities in one polyhedral description.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A critical-region member is nonminimal when removing it does not change the represented optimal-solution mapping anywhere in parameter space.
assumptions_latex: \(K\) is finite.
Each \(\mathcal R_k\) is polyhedral and each \(S_k\) is defined on \(\mathcal R_k\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\bigcup_{j:\theta\in\mathcal R_j}S_j(\theta)=\bigcup_{j\neq k:\theta\in\mathcal R_j}S_j(\theta)\) for every \(\theta\) in the parameter domain.

notation.meaning: solution-map contribution attached to the kth region

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition is internally coherent and fits the leaf, but this exact solution-map family minimality convention has no citation. A direct source is required before choosing it over other meanings of a nonminimal critical region.

children.title: Regional Description Ambiguity
children.top_down_role: Navigation limits caused by nonunique or redundant regional representations.

knowledge_statements.title: Regional Description Ambiguity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nonuniqueness of labels and inequality descriptions for one parameter region.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A critical region is a subset of parameter space, whereas a basis label, complementary partition, or inequality system is a representation of that subset. Thus two systems \(H_1\theta\leq h_1\) and \(H_2\theta\leq h_2\) may define the same polyhedron even when \((H_1,h_1)\neq(H_2,h_2)\), and distinct optimal structures may label the same region. Consequently, syntactic inequality of two descriptions does not imply that their represented regions differ. Canonical output requires an explicit normalization convention, for example irredundant facet inequalities with fixed row scaling and ordering together with a deterministic structure-label rule.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The same critical region may have different inequality systems or optimal-structure labels, so unequal descriptions need not represent unequal regions and canonical output requires explicit normalization.
assumptions_latex: \(H_i\theta\leq h_i\) represents a polyhedron in a common parameter space for \(i\in\{1,2\}\).
Multiple bases or complementary partitions may represent the same optimal regime.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\{\theta:H_1\theta\leq h_1\}=\{\theta:H_2\theta\leq h_2\}\) does not imply \((H_1,h_1)=(H_2,h_2)\).

notation.meaning: an inequality representation of a parameter polyhedron

children.title: Critical-Region Construction Methods
children.top_down_role: Method families for producing explicit parameter-space subdivisions.

children.title: Facet Exploration
children.top_down_role: Traversal between adjacent parameter regions.

knowledge_statements.title: Facet Exploration
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Adjacency traversal of full-dimensional polyhedral critical regions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input a seed parameter \(\theta_0\) with finite optimum and an oracle returning an optimal structure and its polyhedral region. Initialize a queue with the region \(\mathcal R_0\) returned at \(\theta_0\). Repeatedly remove an unprocessed region \(\mathcal R\); for each relative facet \(F\) not on the boundary of the parameter domain, choose \(\theta_F\in\operatorname{ri}(F)\), perturb to \(\theta_F+\varepsilon n_F\) across its outward normal, and query the oracle. Insert every previously unseen returned region and record its adjacency through \(F\). Stop when the queue is empty and output the discovered regions and facet-adjacency graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Starting from one region, cross each unexplored facet, query the neighboring optimal structure, and continue until no new adjacent regions remain.
assumptions_latex: The parameter domain and returned critical regions are polyhedral.
The oracle correctly classifies sufficiently small cross-facet perturbations.
The intended full-dimensional region complex is facet-connected.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The output is the facet-connected component of \(\mathcal R_0\) in the oracle-induced critical-region complex.

notation.meaning: a relative facet of the current region
a sufficiently small positive crossing distance

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm fits the traversal leaf, but no source supports its oracle and facet-crossing model. Degenerate facets, simultaneous boundary crossings, and the conditions ensuring that a perturbation reaches the intended adjacent region require a sourced convention.

children.title: Optimal-Structure Enumeration Family
children.top_down_role: Construction through candidate optimal bases or complementary partitions.

children.title: Optimal-Basis Enumeration
children.top_down_role: Critical-region construction organized through candidate optimal bases.

knowledge_statements.title: Optimal-Basis Enumeration
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exhaustive enumeration of optimal simplex bases over a polyhedral parameter domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(P(\theta)=\min\{c(\theta)^\top x:Ax=b(\theta),\ x\geq0\}\) with \(\theta\in\Theta\), enumerate every set \(B\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}\) satisfying \(|B|=m\) and having nonsingular \(A_B\). Set \(N=\{1,\ldots,n\}\setminus B\), compute \(x_B(\theta)=A_B^{-1}b(\theta)\) and \(r_N(\theta)=c_N(\theta)-A_N^\top A_B^{-\top}c_B(\theta)\), and form \(\mathcal R_B=\Theta\cap\{\theta:x_B(\theta)\geq0,\ r_N(\theta)\geq0\}\). Discard empty regions and retain every nonempty pair \((B,\mathcal R_B)\). After all bases have been tested, output the retained family, optionally identifying equivalent regional solution descriptions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Test every nonsingular basis, retain the parameters where its basic solution and reduced costs are feasible, and output all nonempty basis regions.
assumptions_latex: \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\) has rank \(m\).
\(b:\Theta\to\mathbb R^m\) and \(c:\Theta\to\mathbb R^n\) are affine on a polyhedron \(\Theta\).
Polyhedral emptiness can be decided.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every \(\theta\in\Theta\) for which \(P(\theta)\) has a finite optimum belongs to at least one retained \(\mathcal R_B\).

notation.meaning: parameter region where B is primal-dual feasible

children.title: Complementary-Partition Enumeration
children.top_down_role: Critical-region construction organized through candidate complementary partitions.

knowledge_statements.title: Complementary-Partition Enumeration
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Enumeration by primal-positive and dual-positive index partitions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the primal-dual pair \(Ax=b(\theta),\ x\geq0\) and \(A^\top y+s=c(\theta),\ s\geq0\), enumerate disjoint index sets \((\mathcal B,\mathcal N)\) with \(\mathcal B\cup\mathcal N=\{1,\ldots,n\}\). For each pair, impose primal-dual feasibility, \(x_{\mathcal N}=0\), and \(s_{\mathcal B}=0\), then project the resulting linear system onto parameter space. Retain the partition when the projected region is nonempty; optionally require \(x_{\mathcal B}>0\) and \(s_{\mathcal N}>0\) on its relative interior to identify a maximal strict-complementarity partition. Output all retained regions and their partitions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Enumerate complementary primal and dual index partitions, project their feasibility systems to parameter space, and retain every nonempty projected region.
assumptions_latex: The primal and dual data depend affinely on \(\theta\).
Strong duality holds whenever the tested primal-dual system is feasible.
Exact polyhedral projection and emptiness tests are available.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Each retained parameter satisfies primal feasibility, dual feasibility, and complementary slackness for its recorded partition.

notation.meaning: indices permitted to carry positive primal variables
indices permitted to carry positive dual slacks
